name: Find competitor content gaps from their sitemap with Bright Data, GPT-5.6, Google Sheets and Slack

parameters.content:
## Find the topics a competitor covers and you never have

Their sitemap is a complete public list of everything they publish. So is yours. The difference between the two is a content plan, ranked by how much they have invested in each subject.

### How it works

**`Find The Sitemaps`** asks each `robots.txt` where the sitemap is, because the filename is never the same twice. If robots names none, the usual paths are tried - and the response is checked for real XML, since a guessed path often returns an HTML 404 with a 200 on it.

Most sitemaps are indexes of other sitemaps, and the nesting goes deeper than one level - monday.com takes three hops before a page URL appears. So the walk is a loop with a depth cap, and image, video and tag sitemaps are skipped by name at every level.

**`Find The Gaps`** compares the two sites on slug words rather than on pages - two requests instead of thousands - and ranks the subjects that appear across many of their URLs and none of yours.

**`Loop Over The Gaps`** then fetches only the top few through the **Web Unlocker**, one at a time, so GPT-5.6 can read what they actually published and say what angle they took and whether the subject is worth your time.

Results land in a sheet, a summary goes to Slack, and whoever submitted the form gets the table back in the browser.

### Setup

1. Bright Data: a Web Unlocker zone as a Header Auth credential. Free tier is 5,000 credits a month.

2. An OpenAI credential, a Google Sheets credential and a Slack credential.

3. Paste your sheet URL into **`Log The Gaps`**, with a tab named `gaps`.

4. Open the Form Trigger and copy its URL.

## 1. Two domains, nothing else
Yours and theirs. Everything after this is looked up, so nobody has to know where either site keeps its sitemap.

## 2. Ask robots.txt, do not guess
Measured: `pipedrive.com/sitemap.xml` returns HTML with zero `<loc>`, while its robots names `sitemap-index.xml`. Every site checked used a different filename.

## 3. Check it is XML before parsing it
A 200 carrying `<!DOCTYPE html>` is a soft 404 dressed as a sitemap, and counting `<loc>` in one reads exactly like a competitor who publishes nothing.

## 4. Walk down until there is nothing left
monday.com takes three hops before a page URL appears, so this loops with a depth cap rather than doing a fixed number of rounds.

## 5. Skip what has no topic
Walking pipedrive's index naively picked its image and video sitemaps. Those are excluded by name at every level, along with tag and author files.

## 6. Compare slugs, not pages
This is what makes it cheap. Two sitemaps are two requests and already tell you which subjects exist on one site and not the other.

## 7. Read only the top few
Every article opened is another request. The loop takes them one at a time so a burst never earns the Unlocker's rate-limit reply, which arrives as HTTP 200.

## 8. One judgement, not five
The model rates every subject in a single call and is told to mark a competitor's own product news as low - those are gaps on purpose.

## 9. A row each, a digest once
After the Split Out there is one item per gap, so the last two nodes carry `executeOnce` - a Slack node fed six items posts the same digest six times.

## A gap is not automatically an opportunity

This compares what two sites have published. It does not know whether anybody searches for those subjects, whether the competitor's pages get any traffic, or whether the gap exists because the topic is bad for your business. Plenty of gaps are gaps on purpose.

Slug words are a proxy for topics and a rough one. A site that puts dates or IDs in its URLs will produce noise, and a site that uses short opaque slugs will look emptier than it is. Read the ranked list as a shortlist to check against your keyword tool, not as a plan.

**Cap the reading, not just the comparison.** The slug diff is two requests. Every article the loop opens is another, so `max_gaps_to_read` is the setting that decides what a run costs. Raise it once you have seen one run.

Fetching a competitor's public pages is ordinary competitive research, but their content is still theirs. Use this to decide what to cover, not what to copy.

parameters.formTitle: What do they write about that we do not?
parameters.formDescription: Two sitemaps, compared. Takes a couple of minutes.

parameters.text:
=Two sites in the same market were compared by what they publish. Below are subjects the competitor covers across several pages and you cover on none, with one of their articles for each.

Your site: {{ $json.your_domain }} ({{ $json.urls_yours }} URLs)
Their site: {{ $json.their_domain }} ({{ $json.urls_theirs }} URLs)

For each numbered subject below, write one line in exactly this form:
N | subject in plain words | what angle they took | worth it: high/medium/low | why in under 20 words

Judge 'worth it' on whether the subject looks like something a buyer of this kind of product would search for, not on how well written the article is. Say low when the subject is clearly about their own product, their company news, or their own integrations - those are gaps on purpose.

No preamble, no closing line, no other text.

{{ $json.brief }}
